 Micron Falls 4% as Kioxia’s Cautious Outlook Hits Memory Stocks; Western Digital Drops 5%, SanDisk Slides 3%
 Kioxia's cautious December-quarter forecast rattled memory stocks and raised a question the entire sector is now wrestling with: does soft guidance from Japan's largest chipmaker signal a cooling AI memory cycle, or is the selloff noise ahead of a March…
 By David Moadel 
 Published November 2, 2026, 1:53pm ET · 3 min read 
 Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Kioxia's below-estimate December-quarter guidance sent Micron down 4% and Western Digital down 5%, extending both stocks' month-long losses past 20%.
 Citrini analyst Jukan read Lumentum's sale to Marvell as a signal management expects the AI cycle to collapse within two to three years.
 Kioxia CFO Kawamura called the soft outlook a shipment timing issue, saying AI demand stays robust and next year's output is already sold out.

 A cautious forecast from Kioxia Holdings, Japan’s largest memory chipmaker, turned an overnight gain in Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction ) into a loss and pulled memory stocks lower. Micron stock is at $853.34, down 4% this afternoon. The decline adds to a pullback from an AI-fueled run in the chipmaker’s shares.
 Over the past month, Micron stock is down 20%. That slide comes despite record results: on September 30, the company reported Q4 FY2026 revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379.3% year over year, with an adjusted gross margin of 87%. For Q1 FY2027, Micron forecast its revenue to $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion.

 Kioxia’s Soft Guidance Drags Memory Stocks Lower
 Kioxia Holdings guided its December-quarter operating profit to 2 trillion yen, the company said on November 2. That forecast stands only slightly above the 1.99 trillion yen Kioxia earned in the September quarter, and it came in below analyst estimates. Shares of Kioxia declined in Tokyo as investors digested the outlook.
 The company attributed the soft outlook mainly to shipment timing, saying some orders were pulled into the September quarter while others were pushed into the March quarter. Chief Financial Officer Yoshihiko Kawamura said Kioxia expects a return to rapid growth in the March quarter. He added that AI data center demand remains robust and that Kioxia has sold out its planned output for next year.
 Micron’s slide also follows a weak prior session on October 30, when Samsung missed profit expectations. The open question for the group is whether Kioxia’s outlook signals cooling AI memory demand and pricing, or whether the selling reflects broader tech positioning.
 How Western Digital and SanDisk Stack Up Against Micron
 Western Digital ( NASDAQ:WDC ) stock is at $347.24, down 5%. That’s a steeper decline than Micron’s, making the hard drive maker the weakest of the three. During the past month, Western Digital has lost 24%. The company sells to hyperscalers, cloud service providers and enterprises building out storage for the AI-driven data economy.
 SanDisk ( NASDAQ:SNDK ) stock is at $1,114.65, down 3%. The flash maker is falling less than Micron, which cuts against the idea that Kioxia’s manufacturing partner would take the hardest hit. Across the past month, SanDisk has dropped 36%, the deepest decline in the group, and it declined in the prior session despite upbeat results reported on October 29.
 Why Micron’s Business Model Differs From Its Storage Peers
 Micron makes dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) along with NAND and NOR flash, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI systems . The company’s Strategic Customer Agreements are designed to secure long-term demand visibility, particularly for AI workloads. This mix links Micron to both major memory markets at once.
 Western Digital now operates as a hard disk drive company after separating its flash business into SanDisk, and it keeps an ownership interest in SanDisk. SanDisk, by contrast, designs and makes NAND flash and solid-state drives, producing wafers through Flash Ventures, its joint venture arrangements with Kioxia. That arrangement links SanDisk most directly to Kioxia’s production, while Micron’s DRAM exposure gives it pricing drivers that NAND-focused peers don’t share.
 Micron’s Next Test Is Whether AI Memory Pricing Holds
 Micron’s upcoming earnings report will show whether pricing momentum holds up. On the September 30 call, President and Chief Operating Officer Manish Bhatia said Micron doesn’t have “line of sight to when supply and demand balance.” The company also noted it had “more than 75% of our shipments committed for the year.” Kioxia’s comments on order timing and sold-out output add support to that view.
 Skeptics see a cycle nearing its peak. Analysts’ average revenue estimate for Micron’s fiscal year ending August 2027 is $275.5 billion, a high bar. Citrini Research analyst Jukan has read the sale of Lumentum Holdings ( NASDAQ:LITE ) to Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL ) as a sign that management expects the AI cycle to “collapse in two to three years,” a view that remains one analyst’s take.
 Another weak stretch for the memory group could deepen Micron’s monthly losses, while a pricing update matching Kioxia’s upbeat March commentary could ease the pressure. A cautious approach may make sense until the memory-demand debate resolves.
